video.title: Safe, accountable agents: Permissions, approval and governance
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

chapters.label: The email that went to everyone

scenes.narration: A student's department assistant was asked to remind one student about a deadline. It emailed all three thousand students, using the department's account. No one had to approve it. Who is responsible?
Today: why agents that act need limits, how permissions and human approval keep them safe, and how to teach students to design accountable agent systems.
Once an agent can send, buy or delete, its mistakes become actions in the world. Some actions are reversible and some are not. Safety design starts by sorting them.
Give the agent only the tools and scopes its task needs. A reminder agent needs to email one student, not the whole list. Narrow, per-task permissions turn a disaster into a refused request.
Route irreversible or wide-reaching actions through a human. The agent drafts the message and shows who will receive it. A person approves or rejects it, and the decision is logged.

Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework ask teams to map, measure, manage and govern risks. For agents this means naming who is accountable, logging every action, and planning how to stop the system.

Students tend to add safety at the end, if at all. Make every agent project begin with a short risk review. List each tool, its worst misuse, whether it is reversible, and what limit or approval applies.
Quick check! The assistant can read the timetable, draft a message, and send it to a mailing list. Which action should need human approval?
Sending to the list. Reading and drafting change nothing in the world. Sending is irreversible and reaches thousands of people.
In the app, open the approvals lab. Decide which of the agent's actions to allow, limit or send for approval, and see what happens to each request.
Your turn. Which design would have prevented the email to all three thousand students?
A per-task recipient limit plus human approval for any bulk send. Remember: sort actions by reversibility, give least privilege, route risky actions to a person, and log everything.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: give groups the tool list of a campus assistant agent. Each group fills a table of worst misuse, reversibility and control for every tool. Then compare tables and agree on the approval rules.

checkpoints.prompt: Read the timetable, draft a message, send to a list. Which needs approval?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: it is irreversible and wide-reaching.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: reading and drafting change nothing; sending does.

checkpoints.prompt: Which design would have prevented the email to all students?

options.text: A recipient limit plus approval for bulk sends

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: limits and approval stop the action itself.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: prompts and speed don't restrict what the agent can do.
